title: How an mRNA vaccine works
subtitle: A message that teaches your cells one shape, then disappears

scenes.narration: Your immune system is very good at fighting germs it has met before. The trouble is the first meeting.
scenes.question: How can a message teach your body to fight a virus it has never met?

scenes.title: What the body has to learn
scenes.narration: This is the virus that causes COVID. A shell of fat, with its genes inside, and covered in spikes.

steps.say: The genes are its instructions for making more viruses.
Each spike is a protein. It is the key the virus uses to get into your cells.
It is a chain of 1,273 building blocks, folded into this shape. If your body knew this one shape, it could spot the virus at once.

scenes.title: The message, read and thrown away
scenes.narration: The vaccine does not contain the virus. It holds only a message: the instructions for the spike, written in mRNA.

steps.say: The message is fragile, so it travels wrapped in a tiny bubble of fat.
The bubble merges with the outer skin of a cell near the shot, and slips inside.
There it lets go of the message.
A ribosome, the cell’s protein maker, grabs it and reads it three letters at a time.
For every three letters it adds one building block to a chain, until the whole spike is built.
The cell folds the spikes and carries them out to its surface, where they stick out like flags.
Then the cell breaks the message into pieces and gets rid of it. Its job is done.

steps.say: And notice where the message never went: into the nucleus, where your DNA is kept.

scenes.narration: That is the answer to the most common worry about these vaccines. In the words of the US Centers for Disease Control:
scenes.quote: They do not enter the nucleus of the cell where our DNA is located, so they cannot change or influence our genes.

steps.say: They do not enter the nucleus, where our DNA is kept, so they cannot change our genes.

steps.say: An immune cell drifting past bumps into the spikes, and its sensors happen to fit their shape.
That match tells it to make copies of itself, again and again.
Those new cells pour out antibodies: small Y shaped proteins that grab onto the spike and nothing else.
And some of the copies become memory cells. They stay in your body, and remember the shape.

scenes.title: When the virus arrives
scenes.narration: Later, the real virus gets in. This time your body has met its spike before.

steps.say: The virus lands in your nose and starts looking for cells to enter.
Memory cells recognise its spikes straight away.
They multiply and pour out antibodies much faster than the first time.
The antibodies stick to the spikes, so the key no longer fits a cell’s lock.
The virus is stopped before it can spread far. The message that taught your body is long gone. Only the memory stays.
